utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-03-68-T, The Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Mr. Oric, the usual question which, however, is meant to ensure that your rights are protected. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow this in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you, too. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, senior trial attorney, together with co-counsels Ms. Patricia Sellers, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and as case manager Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I represent the Defence of Mr. Naser Oric. Together with us is Ms. Jasmina Cosic, our legal assistant, and Mr. Geoff Roberts, our CaseMap manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and the rest of your team. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, only the issue you raised yourself regarding the map a few days ago. There is a wish raised, and we monitored that, for a kind of map to be used by the parties, including the Court, of course. And if you want so, I will update you of our findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The map is available, but whenever it becomes detailed, there is this problem of the area, the whole area that covers the indictment. It is the western part of the region that falls apart when it comes to a scale of 1 to 25.000, meaning in short if the Court likes the most detailed map covering most of the hamlets, and of course the villages, but mostly the hamlets, we are more or less obliged to make use of two maps instead of one map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And I learned that it is the wish of the Court to see as much hamlets --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- as possible to clearly use it during the trial. And then we will provide the Court and of course Defence and use our own coloured map, highlighting then the places in the indictment. I don't know how fast the service can be over -- the mapping unit of the Tribunal, but we'll see to it that it will be done quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I would imagine you also have the whole system digitalised, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine so, which I have used in my country. Anyway, I think -- I'm sure that you have done your level best, and that you will be providing us with the best that is available. I have no doubt about that. And that makes us happy. And I suppose that on the part of the Defence, does that make you happy, too?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, with a view to the coming witness, Your Honour, you might wish to update yourself of her specific health situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we need to stay in public on this, or shall we go for a little while in private?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My request is that you do it in private session and ask her about it, and the circumstances, and also the need for perhaps a break not after one hour and a half but after an hour, but you Your Honour can observe that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not a problem with us, for sure. We have sort of been forewarned on this, and we will deal with the issue -- play it by ear. Incidentally, you all know that on Monday, Monday is a UN holiday, and we will not be sitting. I want you to be aware of that. All right. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There is one matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I know my colleague had a brief word with Mr. Wubben on this subject this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon? We are still in public, yeah. Stay in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We want to express our concern to have a definitive witness list for the coming weeks so that we can naturally prepare for next week and the following week, and indeed during the break in November so that we can make good use of that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We definitely need to receive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, once you have brought this matter up, we will be insisting on the Prosecution to do that. But also we have met with our staff, and we have a whole programme of things to be done during the days when we will not be sitting because of my absence from the Tribunal. And it will -- those days will be -- should be very profitable, in fact. I mean, you will get the details from our staff, both of you, and you would also know what we require of you to be done or to do in the course of those two weeks. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with a view to scheduling of the witnesses, it's of course of importance how the response will be to the motions regarding 92 bis and of course our possibility on organising the videolink. What I would -- would like to suggest is that we file tomorrow our list for up to the 2nd of November, and then as soon as possible the week after, our projections for the week after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Incidentally I can inform you that this morning we concluded our deliberations on the Prosecution motion for the issuance of a subpoena testificandum against Witness C002, if I remember well. Of course, that will be handed down in writing because that has to precede a proper subpoena. We can inform you that we have -- we will be granting the motion. So you can take that witness into consideration as well in the scheduling of your witness list. This morning, I signed the decision, the oral -- the verbal -- sorry, the written version of the oral decision on the guidelines, so that is available formally. And I think we should be also in a position today, if it's given to us for the last verification, our decision on the motion for protective measures, Prosecution Motion for protective (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: (Redacted) Registrar. The name of that gentleman needs to be redacted. And that should be signed today. If it's not signed today, it's signed tomorrow. We have again reached a unanimous decision on that as well. But as we had promised you, it will be done in writing rather than verbal. So let's bring the witness in. And as soon as she has sat down, Registrar, after she has sat down, I will need to explain a few things to her. And then we go a little bit in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Madam. I want to make sure, since -- as I am speaking in English, I want to make sure that what I am saying and what will be said inside this courtroom as we go along this morning is being translated to you in your own language. So please tell me if you are receiving interpretation in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning to you. And welcome to this Tribunal. I am the Presiding Judge. My name is Carmel Agius, and I come from the island of Malta, not far away from where you live. To my right, Judge Brydensholt Denmark, from the kingdom of Denmark, and to my left I have Judge Eser from Germany. We are presiding over this trial, and you are one of the witnesses in this trial. We will try to make your life as easy as possible. I will make sure, together with the two Judges, that you will be treated as nicely as possible and that you will feel as comfortable as possible while you are giving evidence. So you don't need to worry. I want you to feel very relaxed. And I am going to explain to you a few things before we start with your testimony. First of all, although you have been brought here as a witness by the Prosecution, you are now, that you are sitting there, a witness of this Tribunal, a witness of this Court. And your duty is to speak the truth, to say the truth, and to say the truth -- answer the truth to every question that is put to you, whether it is put to you by the officer from the Prosecution or whether it is being put to you by Defence counsel. You are old enough and intelligent enough to know that every accused has a right to be represented. And the lawyers representing the accused have a duty to defend their client. So they will be asking you questions, too. And you have a duty to answer those questions fully and truthfully. Now before we proceed any further, our regulations, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. It's like taking an oath. And in this solemn declaration --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' note: Will the witness please speak up or move closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, our Rules require you to enter a solemn declaration. And the text of the solemn declaration is contained in a piece of paper that Madam standing next to you is going to hand to you. Please stand up. Read that text aloud. What I need now is one of the interpreters, do you have a copy of the text? I am going to read it out, Madam. One of the ladies who is in the interpreters' booth will be translating what I will be saying, and please, you repeat the same words. And that will be your solemn undertaking. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare. You need to come near the microphone because the interpreters cannot hear you. I am going to repeat, because I need to hear you make the statement, too. I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare to tell whatever I know and whatever I don't know, I cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just repeat the words that the interpreters will tell you. Just those, don't add words of your own. I'm going to start again. I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will tell you whatever I know and whatever I don't know, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When I speak, the interpreters translate my own words to you. It's only two or three words. The first part of the statement. I don't want you to make a statement of your own. I want you to repeat the words that the interpreters -- you will hear the interpreters tell you. I am going to start again. I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, I thank you. Let's go into private session for a while. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And now we are in open session. From now onwards, you can -- your words will be heard and my words will be heard and the words of everyone else will be heard. We are no longer in private session now. You will first be asked a number of questions by Mr. Wubben. I suppose you have Mr. Wubben already before. And when he finishes, I think Mr. Jones -- Mr. Jones will ask you, who is appearing for Mr. Oric, will ask you a few questions. And then when we finish, that will be over, your ordeal will be over, and you can back home. And we will give you all the assistance that you need so that you arrive home safe and sound. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Wubben:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions to you to ask. Let me start with the first question. Your name is Milenija Mitrovic, and you were born the 10th of September 1949?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your ethnic origin is Serb? And your current occupation is housewife?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I look at the transcript, Your Honour, whether or not her answers had been on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Mitrovic, if you move nearer to the mic, to the microphone, move as near as you can and speak a little bit louder so that the interpreters can hear. Because what happens here is that when I speak in English, the interpreters translate into your language. When you speak in Serbian, the translators will have to translate to us into English. So they need to hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only speak Serbian. I don't speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So speak out when you answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only speak Serbian. I can't speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's good. Thank you. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, Witness, a question regarding the year 1992. And let me take you back to the time after the war started in April 1992. After April 1992, in that year, did you live in the hamlet of Kusici?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the hamlet was surrounded by more hamlets?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that part of a village? What village?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: There were the Serbian villages and the mixed villages. Kusici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about the village. Was this village mentioned Zabokvica village?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Zabokvica, Resavici, Dobrak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what part of what municipality? What was the name of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was the Srebrenica Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where you lived was the hamlet of Kusici, as you stated. And I reiterate that. The Zabokvica, was that --

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Kusici, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- was part of --

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: There was Zabokvica, and there was the village of Kusici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Municipality of Skelani?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Skelani -- was your hamlet part of the Municipality of Skelani or Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was part of the Srebrenica Municipality. There was no Skelani Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village of Skelani was in the neighbourhood of your hamlet?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. No, it wasn't. We are far away from Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the year 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow to lead the questions by me now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you confirmed that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry. It's a matter which I was hoping Your Honour might consider our position as far as leading is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We would be opposed to leading this witness through her evidence, through any of the controversial parts of it in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Controversial, obvious, but the rest usually we allow both parties to lead as much as possible if it speeds up the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. My learned friend has led the witness through the non-contentious parts of her evidence, i.e. Where she lives et cetera. For anything which concerns her account of events in 1992 we feel very strongly that that evidence has to come from this witness, particularly given that she doesn't read or write, and so there isn't a reliable written statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, as we go along, as we go along, Mr. Wubben would indicate if he wants to lead. If you want to object, you object. And then we'll decide, that's how we do it. But the practice is sometimes we allow, sometimes we don't, depending on what kind of questions are being asked and how controversial the point and issue -- point of evidence and issue is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, just to make our position clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the normal position you are taking, Mr. Jones, and it will be dealt with in the normal way that we are used to here. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you lived in the hamlet of Kusici. You confirmed to the Court the Zabokvica village. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, after the war in the year 1992, had there been any incidents related to the war in that particular year or not?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So until the end of the year 1992, everything seems quiet in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in the year after, in the beginning of 1993? Can you clarify that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen in regard to incidents related to the war in the beginning of 1993 in the hamlet you lived?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I was at home when it started. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can remember you were at home. And please tell the Court what started. What did you see or hear?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I was at home. And when it started in 1993, there was an attack and shooting, and I didn't see or hear anything other than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It started in 1993. And was that in your hamlet in the beginning of the year, the first month of the year?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember which year that was. I cannot read or write, so I couldn't follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are still in the year 1993. You confirmed to the Court that the year 1992 was quiet, though there was a war. And in the beginning of the following year, that means January, February, or March 1993, please confirm to the Court, something happened in the hamlet. Do you recall the month?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 16th of January 1993. That's the only thing I can remember. Before that, we had been told for women and children to move out, but I had no place to go to. So when it fell, I don't know anything else apart from that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you confirmed to the Court that there was an attack. Can you tell me more about it, what you saw and what you heard on that specific day?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: At around 5.00 on the morning when the attack started, when they attacked Kusici village, they captured some people and drove them out. But I didn't hear or see anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do after you saw this attack or heard this attack?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. They attacked us. They started shooting, and we started running away. And I didn't see anything else. Everything was left behind in our houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you ran to?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: To the Pirici, Markovici, all the way to the Dobrak hamlet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you meet anyone there?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I met some army people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they look like, those army people?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't recognise anyone. They had balaclavas over their heads. They had ribbons tied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they wear any arms?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- from what country or from what ethnic origin they were?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot say from which country they came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these from Serbian origin, these army?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Why would the Serbs be chasing us away?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you speak about army, do you mean soldiers that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were soldiers, only I don't know who they were. They were in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If they were not Serbian soldiers, were they Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: They were not Serbs. I just don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they do after they met you or you ran into them?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: They didn't do anything. They took over and sat there, and we were there all the time. It was a sunny day, although it was January but it was rather warm. The nights were warm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "they took over"?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: When they took us over, because it was already dark, and one group went to Poljak, and then another one went to another village, and the rest were captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you yourself, were you captured as well?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you the only one who was captured?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, there were a lot of us women from the hamlets of Kusici and Dvizovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What women from the hamlet of Kusici? Can you name them?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Mileva Mitrovic, Stanija Mitrovic, myself, my neighbour Mitrovic, Stana Mitrovic, Mileva Mitrovic from Kusici. And her son, Sane, who was disabled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the following name of this last person you mentioned referred to as Sane, his first name?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Stanko Mitrovic. He was paralyzed in one leg. He used a stick to walk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you taken as well to Poljak subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you stay the night, the evening over there?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we stayed there that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that the following day, and related your statement, that should be the 17th of January, that you reached another town or village?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: We spent the night in Poljak. There was a sack of wheat in a cellar. We spent the night, and then we went to Kragljivode to spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stop, please. Witness, I would like to ask you a question related to this Kragljivode, this village. When you arrived there, did you also spend the night in Kragljivode?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we spent the night at a man's house in Kragljivode when we arrived from Poljak. When we got there, this man said we had to spend the night there. That woman's son had been killed, and he put us in the bathroom. We spent that night in the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you there with your group, with your captured group surrounded by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: We were outside --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were outside. Where did you spend the night in Kragljivode?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: We spent the night at a man's house. I don't remember our soldiers and theirs being there together. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you saw Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: When we spent the night there, when they took us to Kragljivode, then they took us to Karacici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will reiterate the question.

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Kragljivode, did you saw Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: We didn't ask anyone anything, nor did anyone ask us anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you spent --

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Nobody asked us anything. I can't say what I don't know. Nobody asked us anything. They just took us to Karacici from Kragljivode.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is still related to Kragljivode. The next morning, did you met any other person being a Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we spent the night at a man's house in Kragljivode. And he went to Srebrenica with us. An elderly man called Bogdan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was an elderly man. How old was he by then? What is your estimation?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was elderly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Meaning more than 50 or more than 60 years? What is "elderly"?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: He was old. He wasn't young. He was an old man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he dressed like a military man or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: He was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did he came from, this person?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: We found him there when we arrived. And in the morning, he went with us to Karacici. We found him there at that man's house. And he joined us and went with us to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you learn from him when you met him that morning? Where did he came from, from what village?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: The name of the village is Dubrovi [phoen], it's near Jezero up there. Near Jezero, Kragljivode, Stublovi. It's a hamlet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, an elderly person, a Serb called Bogdan in civilian clothes. How did he look like? Can you describe in what state of health he was?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I only saw him once. He was all beaten up. He was all blue in the face. Afterwards, I didn't see him any more. They took away another group, and he wasn't with us any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that village, after that meeting, where did you go to captured by those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Two of us escorted us to Karacici from Kragljivode. We were there. They questioned us there. We spent a long time in Karacici, until 3.00. Then they questioned us, and a man said that -- this was Monday. He said we were going to Srebrenica. A man with a tractor came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the tractor or with the help of that tractor, you went to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: We got the order from Karacici. People were saying among themselves that we were to go by tractor. We went by tractor. There was snow. It was slippery, so from Hadzici Brdo, we went on foot to Jadar, downhill, and they put chains on the tyres. We went down to the asphalt and we went on foot to Jadar. And that evening we arrived in Srebrenica. It was Monday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you brought to in Srebrenica when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived, it was dark. They took us to the headquarters. They listed our names, all of us who arrived that night. Then we got warm. There were lots of us. We spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for answering my question. Now, this building, I have a question. Was this the first time you went to Srebrenica, or did you earlier as a civilian or whatsoever paid Srebrenica a visit?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I think I didn't -- I haven't been there since I was taken prisoner. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I don't mean after you have been taken as a prisoner, but I mean before that. Did you knew the town Srebrenica before?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did go there before when my mother-in-law was ill. There was an outpatients' clinic in Jezero, and they referred her to the health centre in Srebrenica. So I took her there by bus, and she was hospitalised in Srebrenica. She stayed there in hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you know -- you knew already a little bit about the buildings and the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did know it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the building you were taken to, how was it called, this first building you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the name of the building was. Two men arrived in the morning to take us to that prison. It was foggy, and then they took us to where there's a fountain in Srebrenica, to another building, near the municipality. But I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will come to that issue later, to the building near the municipality building. But first, you spent the night in another building, and you earlier referred to it as headquarters. So it was a kind of official building, public building?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. When we arrived, they listed us, and we spent the night in a part of that building. And then they took us -- in the morning, they took us to the other building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that you would like to tell a story. But please be limited to answering my question and the issue I will refer to. When you spent the night in this building, you referred to this first building as headquarters, did the same group of other prisoners were with you?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: When we got there from Poljak, we found all the women who were imprisoned in that building, and we all spent the night there, if that's what you're asking me, from Kusici, from Dvizovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those are the same women as you earlier mentioned the names this morning?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The ones whose names I mentioned from Kusici, I didn't tell you the names of the others from Dvizovici who were in that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please recall the names. Please call them.

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Stanko Obradovic, Milka Obradovic, Mara Obradovic, another woman from Kusici whose last name I don't know, and her daughter, Stojanka Obradovic, Jelka, Danica Markovic. Her brother came to Kusici, and she was there, too. I'd forgotten her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were also interrogated or enlisted in this headquarters building?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: They wrote down our names. They took our identity papers, money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the one who -- the ones who took your identity papers, these were from the army or civilians or police?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who they were. I don't know. They were in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by camouflage uniforms? The same uniforms you noticed when your hamlet had been attacked, or were these other camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: What do I know? They were multicoloured, green. I didn't see any other colours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now we arrive at the other issue you already referred to as being taken another building near the municipality building. That other building you were taken to, was that the next morning?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was on Tuesday. We arrived in Srebrenica on Monday, and then on Tuesday morning, early, we were taken away. It was foggy. It was drizzling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were taken then to a building near the municipality building?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were two buildings. I can't remember now. I've forgotten that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That other building is, as common knowledge, next to it there are several buildings. One of those buildings is the court building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't know, putting matters of common knowledge to the witness. Surely the witness should be asked if she knew what buildings were in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's fine. Mr. Jones --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Otherwise counsel is giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will be doing the same. When it comes to establishing these facts, if it is really something controversial, yes, we will put our foot down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's just that the witness said she has forgotten the buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but again, I mean normally one would try to help the witness. We're talking about someone who has had a stressful life and events.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. We just don't want to give the witness evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, I will not allow Mr. Wubben to give evidence instead of her. But I will certainly allow Mr. Wubben, including yourself and Madam Vidovic, to try and refresh the memory of a witness when it starts failing a little bit, I mean, on matters which are not that crucial, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I may proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you recall that the other building might be the court building or is that another building you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I don't know any more. I don't remember what building we spent the night in, where they took us. In the municipality, in the cellar, were they there? I can't remember at all what building we were in. It was a long time ago. The only thing I know is that in the morning, we were taken there. We brought water. We went to the toilet. And we spent the night there, women. I don't remember. I can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were taken to the building near the municipality building, were you imprisoned there in a room, in a cell?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was a big room, and there were a lot of women inside. There was a window with bars on it to one side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe the room more where you were in, the room with the bars?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I can't write. I'm not literate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Because knowing how to read and write has got very little to do with remembering events in one's life that one has lived.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I can't read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but you need to -- do you need to read to remember where you were kept, how big was the cell or the room, how it was? What was its condition? I don't think you need to read anywhere or to know how to read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were benches. I asked for a fire to be lit and for water to be brought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ever give a description of this location, of this room, to anyone before? Were you asked by anyone, by someone to describe this room before? Say, for example, in your own country, were you interviewed by the court in Zvornik, for example? Do you remember being interviewed by Judge Vaso Eric in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lady from Bratunac, Miloslav, showed him to me. We found him there in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, you might consider to make an observation on her health or her condition. It might be time after an hour to have a break. But that's your decision, of course, and consideration of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Mitrovic, we are going to have a short break. The staff will bring you something to drink. In the meantime, relax and try to remember because these things are very important for us. I mean, we weren't there at the time. You were there. So you need to tell us, give us as much information as you can remember. You don't need to read anything. What you remember, you remember. What you don't remember, you don't remember. And where you don't remember, we will ask you whether you have given statements before to anyone else, for example, to an officer of the Prosecution or to a court in Zvornik or elsewhere, and we will try to read out to you if necessary parts of those statements to try and refresh your memory. But you need to tell us. So have a break. I'm going to give you 30 minutes' break, which should be more than enough for you to relax.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting something less than that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 30 minutes is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think let's start with 30 minutes and then we see. Try to remember because I find it difficult to understand how someone who -- I have read the statements that you have made already, someone who claims to have passed through all these events have forgotten important, important details. I do accept that people do forget, but I think that with a little bit of effort you will try to remember. And if you need us to refresh your memory, tell us and we will try to refresh your memory. We will do it ourselves. We won't even let Mr. Wubben do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know, I know. What I don't know, I don't. I will say what I know, and I can't say what I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We will have a half hour's break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. During the break, I consulted a little bit with the representative of the Victims and Witnesses Unit about the condition of the witness. And it has been suggested to you to allow the representative of the Witness and Victims Unit to sit near the witness while she is giving evidence because she could be of assistance to her, and also of assistance to us if we fail to notice in time when we need to stop or when we need to have a break or if -- she is in a better condition than we are to notice a crisis even before it's coming. But we are in agreement. But we also would like to hear what you have to say in regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we have no objections whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So Madam Usher, please. I thank you for your cooperation. Madam Mitrovic, are you feeling better now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good. Good. Can we proceed? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's proceed on your description of that cell with the bars that you gave to the Judges. My question is, can you please describe this cell, this room.

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: There was a barred window in a corner. The room was smaller than this one that we are in now. And that's where we were. There was a stove in another corner. There were benches. There was a desk also. And that is where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The room was smaller than this room. This is a big room. But how smaller was it? Can you describe in metres, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was somewhat smaller than this one, slightly smaller. It wasn't as big as this one. And only women and children were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think you can safely move to the next question. This is perhaps, if it's still in existence, we'll be able to see this room hopefully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name the women and children that were together with you in that particular room?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat their names. Dostana, Milosava, Andja and Stanija, Stojanka, Jelka, Mara, myself, Stanko was with the men. Dostana, Danica, Stojanka, we were all there in that room, Milena, Stana, Dzivana. Dostana was with her children, with her two children in another room, while Dostana was with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- tell the Court about the daily regime. How was the food? How were the circumstances in your own words while you were imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the conditions were not bad. I cannot say that -- were bad. I cannot say. They were not good. It was difficult to live there. It was winter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was winter. Does that mean that it was cold also inside in your cell?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the women and children suffer from that cold, or were you able to warm it or heat it? Can you tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: There was Ivanka's son, a young boy, who was sent to deliver a letter, and Dostana was down there in a house in Srebrenica. We couldn't heat the room. There were no wooden logs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that it was cold?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have light in your cell?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. There were no lights. Only when they came to see us, they would light candles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there toilet or bathroom facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Mitrovic, we can't hear you. Could you speak into the microphone, please. The question was whether there were any toilets or any bathrooms in the room or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were. There was a toilet inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that building. In the basement where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the circumstances, what did you feel during your stay? What were your feelings about it?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other women and children, how did they feel or tell you how they felt?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was nothing to tell. They told us that we would be exchanged. They used to come and see this Stana Mitrovic because she had wounded. They came twice to visit her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About the daily regime, did you get food on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Not every day. We didn't receive food. They would just bring us a slice of bread and a bowl of soup. But I couldn't eat because my dentures were knocked out as I had been beaten. And we were not able to eat. We just needed enough water to drink. We didn't ask for any bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please bear me a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you ask for any bread? Wasn't it available, or was it available?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: We didn't dare because we didn't know those people. We didn't dare ask for bread because they told us they didn't have enough bread for themselves either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long did you stay in that room together with those women and children? Can you give an estimation in days or weeks?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Three weeks. We were in that room for three weeks. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that time, did there also came another woman or more to that cell to join your group?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Andja came, and the friend of the man - that was on the second night - but Andja was taken to the room where men were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to put forward the question but in private session, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go private session, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will go back to the issue of the circumstances of that time and what you heard and learned of the daily regime. My question is how was life, what did you hear around you?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: What was there to hear? They would come and see us, go where the men were. I heard men being beaten. That Sane Mitrovic was disabled. That was on only one evening, though. It didn't happen again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you hear those sounds, did you conclude -- did you feel that there were more prisoners than only the women together with you in that cell?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many of them there were, sir. I don't know how many of them there were. I wasn't able to see. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard men being beaten. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what did you hear that made you think?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: What do I know? What do I know? I heard them beating them one evening. Afterwards, they didn't do that. They would come and look at us and ask us questions. They didn't say anything more to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you heard those men being beaten, what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was only one night. It didn't happen again. That Stanko was crying out. You could hear him moaning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and women in your cell spoke about it, discuss it, about those noises, those sounds?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were the guards? Did they treat you well?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. If we wanted to go to the toilet in the evening or in the morning, Stana was on a stretcher. She couldn't go to the toilet because she had been wounded. They came to see her, try to get her up, try to get her walking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These guards, did they also belong or look like an army, a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Shouldn't the question be what were they wearing or something of that nature really?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Let's hear what the -- you're perfectly right, Mr. Jones. But the witness was about to answer the question. Let's see if she understood it the way you suggested the question should be phrased in any case, and then we could remedy the question if necessary. Did you understand the question that Mr. Wubben put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear your answer, then, Madam, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say what were they wearing, they were wearing multicoloured uniforms. They would come and see us. We didn't have anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these guards wearing uniforms, were these Serbs or another ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were Serbs or Bosniaks. I don't know who they were. I didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they also, these uniformed guards, did they also visit you in your cell?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was only when they wanted to go to the toilet or have a smoke, then they would take us back. They were in a room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall that besides being treated well by the uniformed guards, also opposite stories? Or can you confirm to the Judges that in general and all the time they treat you right?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: They all treated us right. They would come and say we would be exchanged. They didn't treat us badly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any names of the uniformed guards at the prison or other guards?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall, no. I just recall someone called Salko. He knew Milosava Dostana, he had been a neighbour of hers. I don't know any of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the visitors of your cell, from let's say the people who are in charge in guarding, besides those guards, did also other persons visit your cell and informed you about --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, he can ask -- Mr. Wubben can ask: Did anyone else visit the cell, but then to suggest what they might have said or done is far too leading in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take them one by one, Mr. Wubben. Let's first establish whether there were other persons who went there, and then you can put the relevant question in regard to each one of them, if at all relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did also other persons visit your cell?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Zulfo came to visit us in our cell where we women were. And a certain Miko from Osmac. And a man called Budo from Lovrak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Dobrak. I don't recall anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, can you tell me more about the visit by these men you referred to as --

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you what I know. I told you who came. They came on several occasions, but I don't know what their names were. But those three were the ones who came most often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how often came Zulfo?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: We didn't ask him. He and Miko came to see us. They would say we would be exchanged. They told us not to be afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you knew this Zulfo from before?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. When they took us prisoner, then he came to our cell. Milosava Dostana from Bratunac showed him to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know from what village this Zulfo came from?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. We were far away from there. I can't tell you the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe him.

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: He was tall, dark-haired, stocky. He had a leather jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was tall. What do you mean by tall? Very tall or can you describe?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: He was a tall, heavy-set man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And apart from these three names you gave, did also another person visit your cell?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to rise to my feet. But the witness said those three names, and then said "I don't recall anyone else." She has already answered that question, and in my submission she shouldn't be pushed with the same question. She has answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was not pushing a question forward. It was an open question whether or not she recall, apart from the three men --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She doesn't recall. The incident is closed. Mr. Jones was right. You also had the right to put another question suggesting to the witness to think about her previous question and consider whether she would like to change it, whether on rethinking she could remember someone else. But that's about it. I think, Madam Mitrovic, you don't remember anyone else, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. No. I don't recall anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the women in your cell discuss or informed you about the name of another person?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again, I don't know what my learned friend is trying to get at. She can speak about who visited her. She said the names of the people. She was in the same cell as these women. And now Mr. Wubben is asking again what is going to be a very leading question. He can ask did they discuss matters, what did they discuss? But to put a proposition to her, it's feeding her, or attempting to feed her evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, this is not a question pointing out someone else visiting her, but this was a question whether or not other women discussed with this witness the name of another person, not focussed on visiting, discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Wubben. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Witness, you recalled three names. Apart from that, did the women in your cell discuss with you or inform you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- or mention another name?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Only Dostana pointed out this gentleman to me. He came once, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. she told me his name, and then I saw the other three or four men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: That's all I know. I don't remember anything else. She said that his name was Naser Colic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Naser. And what else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he just looked around and then he left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. What is the name that you told us? Naser? Naser who? What else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what was his surname then, the second name? Naser?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know his last name or where he was from. She didn't tell me. And I didn't inquire much about who he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But before -- I asked you the question because before I heard you say something like Colic or something like that. You didn't just say "Naser" and "I don't know the rest." You said Naser plus either Colic. I couldn't hear you well. That's why I'm asking you to repeat the name again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just heard that that was his name, that's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colic, in other words. Colic? Is it Colic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what this woman told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this gentleman with the first name of Naser came once to your cell?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Dostana pointed him out with that name you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, she did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the gentleman with the surname of -- with the first name of Naser, he didn't stay long?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long? Can you give in minutes?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: He just walked around for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: About 30 seconds. Not longer than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did he walk around?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I was sitting on the bench in the corner under the window. The other women were also sitting on other benches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And where was he walking, please?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Around the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around the cell. You mean in the cell as well? Shall I repeat the question, Witness? My question was: Did he also, this gentleman called Naser, the first name, also came in your cell?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd be grateful if in putting the question my learned friend would not insist on the person being called Naser. It's -- as the witness made clear, she was told by someone else that he was called Naser. And this witness hasn't accepted that he was called Naser, and it's clear from her evidence that she doesn't know who he was. So if he could please phrase it so it's not the suggestion that this witness knows that the man was called Naser.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, the Trial Chamber knows that, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So again, my question is, Witness, will you please answer: Did this person called Naser also came in your cell?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Dostana said that he was, and I didn't inquire much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And did that person then came in your cell?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did enter our cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw him yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how does this person pointed out to you as called Naser looks like?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: How can I tell you? He was of medium height. I was excited, and just took a glance at him. That was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just gave the Court a description of this person called Zulfo, very tall et cetera. Compared to this Zulfo, can you tell more about that other person being called Naser?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And like Zulfo, did this --

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Zulfo was much more heavy-set. This one was of medium height.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told the Court that this person called Naser visited your cell. Did this visit also have to do with the exchange?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear that, only those who had captured us came. And when Zulfo came, where we were, and Miko, and they told us that we shouldn't be afraid and that there was going to be an exchange. And they told us nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the exchange take place?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And may I ask again, after how many -- after how long time in weeks?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: We were there for three weeks, and then one day at around 9.00, we were told to be ready and that there was a lorry coming to pick us up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in the lorry?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. We were in a van and in a lorry, there was a dead volunteer, and attending the exchange were Miko, Budo, and Zulfo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Zulfo's role in this, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he do?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: He said that the exchange would take place. Miko told us that had they had enough bread and wood, that we would have stayed longer. And that women and children were guilty of nothing and that they had to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we proceed on that issue, I would like now to ask you to recollect whether or not there was next to your cell other rooms. Was there a corridor? Can you describe that to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a corridor. Where we were, there was a toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you already confirmed or told the Judges that this Stanko was brought to the men's room, the room of the men. Was that also another room, or was there a corridor between? Can you tell us something about it?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: There was a corridor, and we went from our cell through that corridor to the toilet. And there was another room there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the day of your exchange, you could see more than the time than you were in your cell?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: When they came in the evening to make a list of how many of us there were, then the following morning at around 9.00, a van came to take us to Srebrenica and Skelani. We went out of the building to an asphalt road. We waited for a daughter-in-law and children. We got into the van, and the lorry was driving behind us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the lorry with Zulfo?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was Zulfo sitting?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Miko was at the steering wheel, and he sat next to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This day of the exchange, at what time of the day - was it the morning or the evening - that you left this cell together with the women detained with you? Was it at the morning or...?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: At around 9.00 in the morning. We were told to be ready at that time, and that the van was coming. And Stana was on -- she had sticks, and that's where we waited to be taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I give it a follow up in time. Then you go out of that building where you were imprisoned. What did you saw when you walked out that particular building? Did you walk through a corridor or only to a hall or whatever? Can you describe that for the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we passed through a corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: And then out to that asphalt road. We took Stana slowly. She was on the crutches. And then the van came, and Dostana and her children, and we all boarded the van.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question will be: Who were the women, what were the names of the women and others that had been -- the children, for example, that had been exchanged together with you?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Dostana's daughter-in-law and the children and her little daughter and her grandson. I don't know their names. Then there were Milosava, Andja, Stanija Mitrovic, Danica Markovic, Mara Obradovic, Stojanka, Jelka, Milka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, their last names also. Not only the first name but also the last name of those. So Mara Obradovic, and then you start with Stojanka. As I may --

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Stanka Obradovic, Jelka Obradovic. All their surnames were Obradovic. Stanija and I were Mitrovic, Stana, Milena also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mention also -- as I refer to the transcript, Your Honour, Milka? What was the family name of Milka?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Obradovic. She was also from the village of Visovici [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are the names you can recall, or do you recall more?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: This woman Stojanka, who was with us, her last name was also Obradovic. I also know -- I only don't know Dzivana from Arapovici, her last name and her daughter's last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To finalise, the exchange itself, that went without any problems? Can you describe the exchange of prisoners that happened to you to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: When we boarded the van, they turned the music on. We waited for a long time at Vitez. Then -- it was a nice sunny day. We waited for a long time. And I must say that they put their wounded men on the lorry, then that dead volunteer they put on another lorry. And we stayed for a long time at Vitez. It was a nice day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the last time you saw Zulfo?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Zulfo told us to send greetings to our Srebrenica, that Srebrenica, Skelani would again be mixed municipalities as they had been, and that they would have given us more food had it been available.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I finalise my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. We've just been almost one hour sitting. I don't know, the representative of the unit, whether she would recommend we have another break to give her a rest. Yes. So Madam Mitrovic, look at me, we are going to have another short break so that you can relax further. And then we continue. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, could you give us an indication of how much you require.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Approximately an hour and a half maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: An hour and a half. So okay. We will have a 25 -- is that okay, with you, 25 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To make sure that we finish with this witness today, I know that the interpreters usually insist on a 25 -- and the technicians, a 25-minute minimum. If I tried to suggest a 20-minute break, would you wage war against me? I can't see you behind. The chances are that we will then finish earlier with the witness. Okay. And the technicians are okay as well? The reporter? So we will have a 20-minute break. That will put you in the position that you can certainly finish the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, usher, could you bring the witness in, please. Yes, Madam Mitrovic, Mr. Jones, who is appearing for the accused, will now be putting some questions to you. Mr. Jones, she is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Jones:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Mitrovic, I'll be asking you a few questions now, so you could try to keep your voice up and keep your answers short, that would be very helpful. Now, it's right, isn't it, that you've spoken about these events that you've described today in court, you've spoken about them before to investigators?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that you've done that on two occasions at least? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: About that man?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the account you've given today describing your detention, it's right, isn't it, that you spoke once --

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about four years ago to investigators of this Tribunal about those events. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: When they asked me questions, they asked me how old I was. I've forgotten what the date was. What year it was when I was imprisoned and when I went there, and when they came to me ask me questions about it, I don't remember when that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. I simply want to establish who in the past has asked you questions about these events. It's right, isn't it, that first of all you were asked by the police in Skelani about these events?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. No. A woman asked me questions. They came to ask me questions, but our police from Skelani didn't. No, they didn't ask me anything. As I told the lawyer gentleman, our police didn't ask me anything. I would say if they had. I would say so. But they didn't. Why should I hide anything or lie?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. There's no suggestion that you would. Let's go back to that woman you mentioned. Is that an investigator from this Tribunal, someone from outside Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: You mean Dostana? What woman do you mean? I don't remember that woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said "a woman asked me questions". So what woman would that be who asked you questions about these events?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: I mean, she spoke in a foreign language, and our interpreters interpreted. And she asked me questions, and I made a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So stopping there, we'll assume that that's the investigator of the Tribunal, international. It's right, isn't it, then that you never gave any statement to the Skelani police about these events?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, never. They didn't question me. I would say if they had. I have nothing to hide. Nobody asked me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's also right, isn't it, that as you told us this morning you've never given evidence in a court before in your life?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've never spoken about these events to a judge in your own country?

utterances.speaker: MILENIJA MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, never, never. Never. I never did. I never knew what a court was. I'm not literate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we're talking of an investigative judge. And in various parts of civil-law countries, the interviewing of individuals most of the time is not conducted in proper courtrooms or in those conditions. I mean, most of the time, it's conducted in the judge's own room.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
